segments.text: This afternoon somebody at the Nest has emptied a whole wallet onto the shared table and laid every note in a straight line, the oldest and most crumpled at one end and the crispest at the other, with a single cowrie shell at the head of the row like a chairman, and beside it a yellow sticky note carrying one word, in capital letters: Switzerland. Whose wallet it is, I will tell you before we close. Chale, how the thing dey go? I am Kofi, the Editor, this is the Gold Coast Palava, and this fourth edition costs about fifty megabytes, which, since the thing be say we all no dey hold, is the one price on this paper the cedi cannot change. If you have not watched our first two editions, go back for them first, because the gold Asante owed Britain in the first, and the gold scheme I promised to put a price on in the second, both come back today to collect their bill.

Page one, and as the house rule goes, every headline is a question. Our lead: how did a little sea shell, carried here from islands in the Indian Ocean, give its name to the money in your pocket? Is the cedi really printed in Switzerland, as your uncle swears at every funeral? How did Ghana create billions of cedis in 2022 without switching on a single printing press? Why, from December, will Kwame Nkrumah be the only one of the Big Six left on our money? And tucked in the corner like a classified ad: which empire's money did Ghana throw away for decimals almost six years before that empire did the same thing at home?

Do you remember the gold of our first edition? In Twi, gold and money share one word, sika, because for centuries on this land money was gold dust, weighed on small brass scales against little cast figures we now call goldweights, and the smallest weight in that system was the pesewa, so the coin in your pocket is, by its very name, a pinch of gold. But gold was for big deals, and for buying fish there were cowries, the small white shells the Akan called sedie, and they did not come from our beaches: most were gathered in the Maldives, islands in the Indian Ocean, and carried to West Africa in the holds of European ships, often as ballast, in a trade that also bought human beings. Then, in the second half of the eighteen hundreds, merchants shipped in so many cheaper shells from East Africa that the cowrie lost most of its value along the West African coast, and that, my people, is the first inflation in this story: too many shells chasing too few goods. The British replaced shells with shillings. From nineteen twelve a West African Currency Board, sitting in London, issued one currency for Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Sierra Leone and the Gambia, backed by reserves held in London, so the colony's money was only as free as London allowed. On the fourteenth of July nineteen fifty-eight, sixteen months after independence, the new Bank of Ghana issued the Ghana pound, our own notes at last, but still pounds, shillings and pence, until Nkrumah decided that a free country should count in tens.

On Monday the nineteenth of July nineteen sixty-five, in the cool, grey middle of the rainy season, when Accra wakes under low cloud and the open gutters still hold the night's rain, Ghanaians queued at bank counters with pound notes in their hands to meet a new money: the cedi, named after the sedie, the cowrie, and divided into a hundred pesewas, the old gold weight. One cedi was worth eight shillings and four pence, one Ghana pound bought two cedis and forty pesewas, and on the front of every note was one face, the President's, Kwame Nkrumah's. In the silent film of those queues, people hold the new notes up to the light, as if checking whether freedom had a watermark. Four days after the cedi was born, in Washington, President Lyndon Johnson signed a law taking the silver out of America's dimes and quarters, because the silver had become worth more than the coins it was stamped into: two countries in one week, both admitting that money is a promise, not a metal. Nkrumah's cedi lived nineteen months. After the coup of February nineteen sixty-six, the soldiers of the National Liberation Council issued a New cedi on the seventeenth of February nineteen sixty-seven, one new cedi for one cedi and twenty pesewas, with Nkrumah's face removed; on the ninth of March nineteen seventy-nine another military government changed the notes again and kept thirty percent of the cash you brought to the counter, and half of anything above five thousand cedis; and by two thousand and seven the biggest note, twenty thousand cedis, was worth about two dollars, so on the first of July two thousand and seven four zeros were cut off and ten thousand old cedis became one Ghana cedi.

Now the palava your uncle started: is the cedi printed in Switzerland? Here is the record. The Bank of Ghana does not print its notes at home; it buys them from a tiny club of security printers, fewer than twenty in the whole world by the count of its currency head, Dominic Owusu. For years the main printer was De La Rue in Britain, and a former deputy governor, Emmanuel Asiedu-Mante, said Ghana had also used firms in Germany and France. The hundred- and two-hundred-cedi notes of twenty nineteen, and the five-cedi note for our sixtieth anniversary, were printed by an American company, Crane Currency, which beat five rivals, among them, yes, a Swiss one, Orell Füssli of Zurich. For the new notes launched this month, the Bank has not publicly named the printer. So there is no public record of the cedi being printed in Switzerland; the nearest Switzerland comes is the ink, because one Swiss company, SICPA, near Lausanne, supplies the security inks on most of the world's banknotes, though whether that includes ours is not public. But chale, that question is staring at the wrong machine. Most cedis are never printed at all: Ghanaians moved four point five four trillion cedis on mobile money in twenty twenty-five alone, and new money is created whenever the Bank of Ghana lends. In twenty twenty-two it lent the government, through an overdraft, about seven percent of everything the economy produced, created with keystrokes. That year the cedi lost about thirty percent against the dollar, inflation reached fifty-four point one percent in December, so a hundred cedis bought what sixty-five had bought a year earlier, and on the nineteenth of December Ghana stopped paying most of its foreign debts. If you asked "how machay be the plantain?" that year and flinched, you had met monetary policy. Monetary policy, plainly, is the Bank of Ghana setting the price of money. Its policy rate is what banks pay to borrow from it; raise it and loans cost more, spending slows and prices calm down; cut it and money gets cheaper. After twenty twenty-two that rate climbed to thirty percent, the IMF lent three billion dollars under a programme Ghana completed on the twenty-seventh of July this year, inflation fell to five point five percent in October, and on the eighteenth of November the Bank cut its rate from fourteen to eleven percent. And the bill I promised you in our second edition: the IMF says the Bank's gold-purchase programme lost more than one point seven billion dollars in twenty twenty-five, while also crediting it with strengthening the reserves; the Bank of Ghana and GoldBod have defended the programme and disputed how its losses were described. We print both, and you weigh them.

Then, in nineteen sixty-five, there was one face on every note; now, on Thursday the twelfth of November twenty twenty-six, at Bank Square in Accra, President Mahama launched the Heritage Series: eight notes, eight faces. Agnes Tagoe-Quarcoopome, remembered as the first Makola trader to open a bank account, on the one cedi; Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery on the two; Kwegyir Aggrey on the five; Justice Annie Jiagge on the ten; the composer Ephraim Amu, the second of the two men our Amo, The Discerning, is named after, on the twenty; Theodosia Okoh, who designed our flag, on the fifty; Kofi Annan on the hundred; and on the two hundred, the face the soldiers removed in nineteen sixty-seven, now the only one of the Big Six left on our money, Kwame Nkrumah. The notes stay on cotton, not plastic, because of our heat, they are smaller, they carry features to help people with sight loss tell them apart, and from the first of December they circulate beside the old notes, which stay legal tender. The palava came within a day. Theodosia Okoh's nephew said the face on the fifty looked more like her sister, Dr Letitia Obeng; the Bank replied on the thirteenth that the portrait was built from photographs of Theodosia Okoh herself; and the Minority in Parliament wants to know what the whole exercise cost. And the money in your own pocket? It has never been easier to move money, and it is no easier to keep its value: a three-month treasury bill now pays about four and a half percent a year while prices rise by about five and a half, so money that sits still is quietly shrinking. And here is the item in the corner of page one. Ghana dropped pounds, shillings and pence for the decimal cedi in July nineteen sixty-five, and Britain itself did not go decimal until the fifteenth of February nineteen seventy-one, so the colony counted in tens almost six years before the empire did. E no be small thing.

Back at the Nest, the wallet on the shared table belongs to Kwame, The Combative, who arrived this morning with a bet: his uncle had told him the cedi is printed in Switzerland, so he emptied his wallet and held every note up to the window, looking for the words "Made in Switzerland", and found a watermark, a security thread and no country at all. When Baaba, The Ascendant, slid the Crane Currency story across to him, he clung to the ink, and I let him keep half a point; then I told him the Bank of Ghana begs us not to crumple, staple or spray our notes at parties, and The Combative, who had planned a money bouquet for a friend's birthday, went quiet, smoothed every note flat with the side of his hand and put them back in his wallet one by one, the oldest last. I will tell you more about Kwame in good time.

When I read psychology, the lesson that stayed with me was that a promise is only as strong as the number of people who believe it, and a banknote is exactly that, a promise printed on cotton. Britain or America can print the paper; only we can print the belief, and every government that spends faster than it earns is spending that belief.

Letters Page, and this week's question asks for a lesson: when prices rise faster than your savings earn, what is one thing you, your family or your susu group does to stop your money from shrinking? Tell us in the comments, and I will pin the most useful answer.

That is the fourth edition of the Gold Coast Palava, complete, checked, stamped, priced at about fifty megabytes, filed and signed at The Nest, 266 Sandpiper Loop, Onipa Enclave and dispatched to Accra, to Kumasi, to Bunkpurugu, to Half Assini and to the world. Squad, better time.
